q: Nuclear energy now provides about _____ of the world's electricity from about 450 nuclear power reactors.
e: Nuclear power accounts for approximately 10% of global electricity generation.

q: A nuclear reaction is a process in which a particle or a gamma radiation penetrate into a nucleus and changes its _____.
e: A nuclear reaction alters the configuration of the atomic nucleus.

q: From energy point of view, there are two types of nuclear reactions: exothermic reaction and _____ reaction.
e: Nuclear reactions are classified as exothermic (releasing energy) or endothermic (requiring energy).

q: If the total mass before a nuclear reaction takes place is greater than the total mass after reaction, this mass defect is released as energy and this type of reaction is known as _____ reaction.
e: Exothermic nuclear reactions release energy due to a loss of mass (mass defect).

q: If the total mass before a nuclear reaction takes place is less than the total mass after reaction, external energy must be provided for the reaction to take place, known as _____ reaction.
e: Endothermic nuclear reactions require an input of energy because the products have more mass than the reactants.

q: When a neutron strikes and penetrates a nucleus of uranium-235, the nucleus becomes highly unstable and splits into two lighter nuclei, shooting out two or three neutrons; this splitting process is called _____.
e: Nuclear fission is the process where a heavy nucleus splits into lighter nuclei.

q: For a chain reaction to be maintained, the uranium-235 has to be above a certain _____ mass.
e: A minimum amount of fissile material, called the critical mass, is required to sustain a chain reaction.

q: The energy released per atom in a nuclear reaction is about a _____ times greater than the energy released per atom from a chemical reaction.
e: Nuclear reactions release roughly a million times more energy per atom than chemical reactions.

q: Nuclear reactor is a device in which a fission chain reaction can be initiated, maintained and _____.
e: Nuclear reactors are designed to safely control the rate of the fission chain reaction.

q: Fissionable nuclear fuel is the material for fission reaction to take place, and _____ or plutonium-239 can be used as fuel.
e: Uranium-235 and plutonium-239 are common fissile materials used as nuclear fuel.

q: Neutrons released from a fission reaction are fast neutrons and they need to be slowed down to maintain a chain reaction by a material called _____.
e: Moderators slow down fast neutrons so they can effectively cause further fission.

q: Graphite and ordinary water as well as heavy water are used as _____ in a nuclear reactor.
e: Materials like graphite and water act as moderators to thermalize neutrons.

q: Water and carbon dioxide $CO_2$ gas are used as _____ in a nuclear reactor.
e: Coolants transfer the thermal energy generated by fission away from the reactor core.

q: Control rods are used to control the rate of reaction by raising or lowering them from the core, and boron and _____ are used as control rods.
e: Boron and cadmium are excellent neutron absorbers, making them ideal for control rods.

q: Reactor vessel is to contain the reactor core, moderator, coolant and control rods, and it is a pressurized _____ vessel.
e: The reactor vessel is a robust, pressurized steel container.

q: Shielding is a protective barrier, usually a dense material, which reduces the passage of radiations from radioactive materials by _____ them.
e: Shielding materials absorb harmful radiation to protect the environment and personnel.

q: After three or four years in a reactor, spent fuel must be removed and replaced with a new one because the amount of uranium-235 in it has fallen and the fission products has _____.
e: Fission products accumulate in the fuel rods over time, absorbing neutrons and hindering the chain reaction.

q: Many of the fission products are radioactive and dangerous, and strontium-90 becomes concentrated in the _____.
e: Strontium-90 chemically resembles calcium and accumulates in human bones.

q: Iodine-131 is a dangerous fission product that becomes concentrated in the _____ gland.
e: The thyroid gland actively absorbs iodine, making it highly susceptible to iodine-131 radiation.

q: Many of the fission products are radioactive and dangerous to be released into the environment, and these include strontium-90, iodine-131 and _____.
e: Plutonium-239 is a highly toxic and radioactive byproduct of nuclear reactors.

q: In an atomic bomb, an uncontrolled chain reaction takes place so that an extremely large amount of energy is released in a short interval of time, and when completely fissioned, 1 kg of uranium-235 releases energy equivalently produced by _____ tons of TNT.
e: The fission of 1 kg of U-235 yields energy equivalent to 17 kilotons (17,000 tons) of TNT.

q: The detonation of an atomic bomb releases enormous amounts of thermal energy, achieving temperatures of several million degrees Celsius, which creates a large fireball and a characteristic _____-shaped cloud.
e: The convection currents from a nuclear explosion create a distinct mushroom-shaped cloud.

q: The greenhouse gas emissions from nuclear fission power are much _____ than those associated with coal, oil and gas.
e: Nuclear power plants do not emit carbon dioxide during operation, resulting in much smaller greenhouse gas emissions.

q: A catastrophic risk potential in nuclear reactors can be brought about by overheated fuels melting and releasing large quantities of fission products into the environment, which is known as _____.
e: A nuclear meltdown occurs when fuel rods overheat and melt, breaching containment.

q: The 1979 Three Mile Island accident and 1986 _____ disaster ended the rapid growth of global nuclear power capacity.
e: The Chernobyl disaster in 1986 severely impacted public perception and the growth of nuclear power.

q: A release of radioactive materials followed the 2011 Japanese tsunami which damaged the _____ Nuclear Power Plant.
e: The 2011 tsunami caused a severe nuclear accident at the Fukushima I plant.
